# Aṇḍabhūtajātaka (Ja 62)

**ID:** Ja 62
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Aṇḍabhūtajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Blindfolded Husband
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja62
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Aṇḍabhūtajātaka* (also spelled *Andabhūtajātaka* or *Andhabhūtajātaka*; Jātaka 62) is preserved in the Ekanipāta (Itthivagga) of the Pali Jātaka collection (PTS 1: 289–295) [Fausböll 1877; Cabezón 2017]. In English, it has been translated by Bhikkhu Sujato under the title *The Blindfolded Husband* [SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the story of the past to a monk distressed by lust, warning that women cannot be safeguarded against misconduct [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta is a gambling king who remains undefeated in dice by reciting a truth-utterance asserting the fickle nature of womankind [Appleton 2010; Strickmann & Faure 2005]. Seeking to counter the king's claim, his royal chaplain raises a female child from infancy in total isolation and purity, subsequently amending the king's gaming chant to except his wife [Strickmann & Faure 2005; Cabezón 2017]. The king schemes to smuggle a young man into her chambers; the seduced wife then convinces her blindfolded husband to play the lute while her lover strikes his head, prompting the canonical verse: *Yaṁ brāhmaṇo avādesi vīṇaṁ sammukhaveṭhito…* ("Because the brahman played the lute with his face wrapped...") [Berkwitz, Buddhist manuscript cultures; Fausböll 1877; Cabezón 2017].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports canonical parallels or automated cross-corpus matches for this jātaka [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. However, an unglossed verse in the prose describing conditions for misconduct shows textual overlap with *Milindapañha* 205 [von Hinüber 1994]. The text was early translated and discussed by Richard Pischel [Winternitz 1933]. Material evidence of its early popularity survives at the Bhārhut stūpa, where a bas-relief depicts the minister playing his seven-stringed harp, labeled not by narrative title but by the opening pāda of its canonical verse (*[yaṁ brāhmaṇo a]vāvasi jātakaṁ*) [Berkwitz, Buddhist manuscript cultures; Appleton 2010; Cunningham 1879]. In modern Theravāda reception, it was one of ten jātaka tales selected for dramatization and broadcast on Sri Lankan national radio in 1997 [Appleton 2010].
